cards.explanation: The answer is that they drive him out. Gilead's wife bore him sons, and when they grew up they drove Jephthah out (Judges 11:2). They told him he would have no inheritance in their father's house. I think that one hurt, friends.

The word is woman. The brothers said, “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house, because you are the son of another woman.” (Judges 11:2). His father was Gilead, but his mother wasn't Gilead's wife. That's the line they drew, and it was a cold one.

The answer is a band of worthless men. Out in the land of Tob, “…worthless men gathered around him and traveled with him.” (Judges 11:3). That's the text's description of them, not mine, friends. Jephthah himself is called a mighty man of valor back in verse 1.

The answer is the elders of Gilead. They went to get Jephthah from the land of Tob (Judges 11:5). Later Jephthah asks them, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house?” (Judges 11:7). I think that made for an awkward knock on the door.

The word is commander. The elders said, “Come, be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:6). They were asking him to lead the fight. Verse 1 already calls Jephthah a mighty man of valor.

The answer is why they come to him now in their distress. Jephthah asks the elders, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house? Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?” (Judges 11:7). Honestly, friends, I can't blame the man for asking.

The word is leader. The elders told him he could “…become leader over all of us who live in Gilead.” (Judges 11:8). That's a bigger offer than the first one, which was only to be their commander. They sweetened it, friends.

The answer is True. Jephthah asked, “If you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me, will I really be your leader?” (Judges 11:9). The man wanted it clear before he said yes. If someone had hurt you once, you'd read the fine print too.

The answer is that they call the LORD their witness. The elders said, “The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say.” (Judges 11:10). They didn't just say it, they put the LORD's name on it. After that, the next step was for Jephthah to go with them.

The answer is False. Judges 11:11 says Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, the people made him leader and commander, and he “…repeated all his terms in the presence of the LORD at Mizpah.” Tob was behind him by then. Mizpah is the place to remember, friends.

The answer is that he asks what the king has against him. Jephthah's messengers say, “What do you have against me that you have come to fight against my land?” (Judges 11:12). The Ammonites are already at war with Israel, and he asks what's behind it. Straight to the point, and I like it.

The answer is to give it back peaceably. The king says, “Now, therefore, restore it peaceably.” (Judges 11:13). He says peaceably, but he's already come to fight. That's a polite word on top of an army, friends.

The answer is False. Jephthah's message says, “Israel did not take away the land of Moab or of the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:15). He doesn't admit a thing, friends. Then he starts walking the king through the history to back it up.
The answer is that both kings refuse. The king of Edom “…would not listen.” and the king of Moab “…would not consent.” (Judges 11:17). Two doors, two closed. So Israel stayed in Kadesh.

The word is border. Israel camped on the other side of the Arnon but “…did not enter the territory of Moab, since the Arnon was its border.” (Judges 11:18). Israel stayed on the other side of the line. Jephthah is making a point about the land, friends.

The answer is True. Judges 11:20 says, “…Sihon would not trust Israel to pass through his territory.” Sihon was king of the Amorites, and he ruled in Heshbon. Israel had asked politely, and he still said no.

The answer is that the LORD gives Israel the win. “…the LORD, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, who defeated them.” (Judges 11:21). Sihon had gathered all his people at Jahaz, and it didn't matter. Israel then took possession of all the land of the Amorites who inhabited that country.

The point is that each side keeps what its god grants. Jephthah asks, “Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us.” (Judges 11:24). Chemosh is the god Jephthah names as the king's. He sets what Chemosh grants the king beside what the LORD has granted Israel.

The answer is three hundred years. Jephthah says, “For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, as well as all the cities along the banks of the Arnon.” (Judges 11:26). That's a long time, friends. Then he asks, “Why did you not take them back during that time?” (Judges 11:26).

The word is Judge. Jephthah says, “May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” (Judges 11:27). He says he has not sinned against the king, and he asks the LORD to decide. He's laid out his case and leaves it there.

The answer is False. The text says the king of the Ammonites “…paid no heed to the message Jephthah sent him.” (Judges 11:28). Jephthah gave his full case, and the king brushed it off. This story isn't over, friends.
